newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. official to study "oil-for-food" in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.N. official to study "oil-for-food" in Iraq.

text.p: Under-Secretary General Yasushi Akashi, who heads U.N. humanitarian affairs, will arrive in Baghdad on Saturday to observe implementation of the "oil-for-food" programme for Iraq, a U.N. spokesman said on Wednesday.
The programme went into operation last December to enable Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies. It expires on June 7.
Secretary-General Kofi Annan is to submit a report before then to the Security Council, which must decide whether the programme should be renewed for another six months.

The council is expected to give its consent but not to agree to a recent call by the Iraqi official who negotiated the oil deal, Abdul Amir al-Anbari, for the oil sales to be doubled to $4 billion over the next six-month period.
The "oil-for-food" programme is intended to offset some of the effects on ordinary Iraqis of sanctions imposed on Iraq shortly after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Akashi, who is also the U.N. relief coordinator, is due in Baghdad May 3 and is expected to spend about six days in Iraq.

He will meet Iraqi government officials and U.N. staff and visit the north of the country, where the United Nations is responsible for distributing humanitarian supplies in three largely Kurdish-inhabited governorates.

"He will be observing first-hand the implementation of the 'oil-for-food' programme in Iraq and reviewing the functioning of the distribution system for humanitarian goods as well as the observation mechanisms in place there," the U.N. spokesman said.
He was referring to U.N. monitoring to ensure the supplies are distributed fairly and reach all sectors of the population.

While the oil sales have gone smoothly, Iraq has frequently complained that the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee has been sluggish in approving contracts for the purchase of humanitarian goods. The first food shipments began arriving in Iraq at the end of March.
